verses.text: The man knew  Eve his wife. She conceived,  and gave birth to Cain, and said, “I have gotten a man with Yahweh’s help.”
Again she gave birth, to Cain’s brother Abel. Abel was a keeper of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground.
As time passed, Cain brought an offering to Yahweh from the fruit of the ground.
Abel also brought some of the firstborn of his flock and of its fat. Yahweh respected Abel and his offering,
but he didn’t respect Cain and his offering. Cain was very angry, and the expression on his face fell.
Yahweh said to Cain, “Why are you angry? Why has the expression of your face fallen?
If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.”
Cain said to Abel, his brother, “Let’s go into the field.” While they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel, his brother, and killed him.
Yahweh said to Cain, “Where is Abel, your brother?” He said, “I don’t know. Am I my brother’s keeper?”
Yahweh said, “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the ground.
Now you are cursed because of the ground, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand.
From now on, when you till the ground, it won’t yield its strength to you. You will be a fugitive and a wanderer in the earth.”
Cain said to Yahweh, “My punishment is greater than I can bear.
Behold, you have driven me out today from the surface of the ground. I will be hidden from your face, and I will be a fugitive and a wanderer in the earth. Whoever finds me will kill me.”
Yahweh said to him, “Therefore whoever slays Cain, vengeance will be taken on him sevenfold.” Yahweh appointed a sign for Cain, so that anyone finding him would not strike him.
Cain left Yahweh’s presence, and lived in the land of Nod, east of Eden.
Cain knew his wife. She conceived, and gave birth to Enoch. He built a city, and called the name of the city, after the name of his son, Enoch.
To Enoch was born Irad. Irad became the father of Mehujael. Mehujael became the father of Methushael. Methushael became the father of Lamech.
Lamech took two wives: the name of the first one was Adah, and the name of the second one was Zillah.
Adah gave birth to Jabal, who was the father of those who dwell in tents and have livestock.
His brother’s name was Jubal, who was the father of all who handle the harp and pipe.
Zillah also gave birth to Tubal Cain, the forger of every cutting instrument of brass and iron. Tubal Cain’s sister was Naamah.
Lamech said to his wives, “Adah and Zillah, hear my voice. You wives of Lamech, listen to my speech, for I have slain a man for wounding me, a young man for bruising me.
If Cain will be avenged seven times, truly Lamech seventy-seven times.”
Adam knew his wife again. She gave birth to a son, and named him Seth, saying, “for God has given me another child instead of Abel, for Cain killed him.”
A son was also born to Seth, and he named him Enosh. At that time men began to call on Yahweh’s name.

footnotes.content: Eve speaks with gratitude, attributing the gift of a son to Yahweh's help. It is a sweet moment after the fall, when grace still prompts a mother to look up and thank the One who gives life.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two brothers, two callings. Abel keeps sheep, Cain tills the ground - both honest work ordained before sin twisted things. Yet from these same callings will come the first worship and the first murder.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In time, Cain brings an offering from the fruit of the ground. The heart of worship is not merely bringing something, but bringing it with the right heart toward the God who gave it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abel brings the firstborn and the fat - the best of what he had. By faith, as Hebrews later testifies, he offered a more acceptable sacrifice. God looks first to the faith behind the offering.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God's respect falls on Abel and his offering, but not on Cain. The anger that rises in Cain shows us how bitter rejection can become when we care more about our offering being accepted than about being accepted by grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh gently asks Cain why he is angry. The God who knows all still stoops to reason with a wayward heart, giving him a chance to turn back before he falls further.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sin is pictured as a crouching predator at the door, eager to master Cain. Yet the command is clear: he is to rule over it. The battle for the heart is real, and God calls us to resist what longs to devour us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: With a word of brotherly invitation, Cain draws Abel into the field. What began in jealousy ends in murder - a sobering reminder of how quickly unchecked sin runs its course.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God asks Cain the same question He asked Adam: 'Where are you?' Though Cain lies, the God who seeks still questions the sinner. Our first instinct is to hide, but the Lord pursues us with piercing questions of mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The voice of Abel's blood cries from the ground to Yahweh. From the first martyr, we see that innocent blood is not forgotten - a truth that points to the blood of Christ, which speaks a better word than Abel's.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The very ground that received Abel's blood now brings a curse on Cain. Creation itself bears witness against the violence of man, groaning under the weight of sin he has brought into it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The farmer who loved the ground finds the ground will no longer yield to him. What he hoped to gain by violence he loses in fruitfulness. Sin always takes more than it promises.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cain finally sees the weight of his punishment and calls it unbearable. True conviction comes when we stop making excuses and begin to see our sin as it really is before a holy God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Banished from the ground's blessing and hidden from Yahweh's face, Cain fears for his life. The greatest terror for the sinner is not death, but being cut off from the presence of God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even in judgment, mercy restrains. God puts a mark of protection on Cain, vowing sevenfold vengeance. Though exiled, he is not yet abandoned - a small glimpse of longsuffering grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cain goes out from Yahweh's presence into the land of Nod, the land of wandering. How tragic to leave the only place of refuge to live as a fugitive from the God who still showed mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In wandering, Cain builds a city to find security apart from God. Man tries to replace the shelter of God's presence with walls of his own making, a pattern that has never ceased.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In Lamech's line we see civilization advancing - cities, livestock, music, and metalwork. Yet the same line boasts of greater vengeance, showing that human progress apart from God only multiplies the cruelty of sin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God gives Adam and Eve another son in place of Abel. Seth becomes the godly seed through whom the call to know Yahweh will be preserved, pointing us to the One greater than Abel who will crush the serpent's head.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At the very moment when sin seemed to have the upper hand, men begin to call on Yahweh's name again. Readers today hear an echo of that longing - after wandering far from God, our hearts still turn back to call upon the name of our only refuge. As of 2026-10, I am grateful that He still hears.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
